failures.criterion: Spec, What this issue delivers: "The broker-wide limit itself is halved, so two pods together cannot send more metadata traffic than one pod was allowed to" — and api/limits.go's own claim that "replicas x this rate ... is the whole fleet's cap" and that GCP's figure leaves "the same 120 a minute the one-pod figure allowed".
failures.evidence: The fleet's secret-store traffic doubled; it was not held. Halving bounds the fleet's HTTP rereads, but the fan-out makes every accepted reread cost one store read on EVERY pod, so the store sees replicas x rate x replicas = N^2 x rate. Measured on two hand-started cmd/broker binaries on one Postgres, with BROKER_TRUSTED_PROXY_HEADER=X-Forwarded-For and a flood from a fresh address each call (the flood spread over addresses this bucket exists for), 20 s: each pod accepted 42 rereads (2.1/s, the halved cap) and each pod made 84 store reads (its own 42 plus its peer's 42) = 168 fleet store reads in 22 s = 7.64/s, against the 4.00/s one pod alone was allowed (DefaultRereadOverallLimit at the base, Every 250ms, one store read per reread). The GCP figure has the same shape: GCPRereadOverallLimit 0.5 reread/s per pod x 2 pods x 2 store reads per pod = 2 rereads-worth a second against the 1/s (120 metadata reads a minute of the project's shared 600) one pod was allowed, so 240 a minute. Red test: packages/envoy/cmd/broker/multiprocess_test.go, TestTwoBrokers/7_TheFleetsStoreTrafficStaysInsideWhatOnePodWasAllowed, in commit 83e394c11d93. It measures the per-reread fleet cost against two real processes and then does the arithmetic on the live limits, so it is not a restatement of a constant. Fails now: `cd packages/envoy && go test -tags multiprocess -count=1 -run 'TestTwoBrokers/7' ./cmd/broker` reports "api.DefaultRereadOverallLimit lets each of 2 pods accept 2.00 rereads a second, and one accepted reread costs the fleet 2 store reads, so the fleet reads the store 8.00 times a second; one pod alone was allowed 4.00" and the same for api.GCPRereadOverallLimit (2.00 against 1.00). The divisor is the replica count squared, not the replica count: Every 1s (Default) and Every 4s (GCP) make it pass, which was verified by applying exactly that change to a scratch copy of limits.go, running the row green, and restoring the file.

failures.criterion: Spec, What this issue delivers: "A reread reaches every pod serving the same database, so a narrowing retag is enforced everywhere within seconds rather than at the next five-minute reload."
failures.evidence: A pod that is draining takes no reread at all, while it goes on being sent requests. cmd/broker/main.go runs the listener on the signal context (`go (&reread.Listener{...}).Run(ctx)`, main.go:175-182), which signal.NotifyContext cancels on the first SIGTERM, so the listener stops the instant the drain begins — and the five-minute reload (policy.NewCurrent's loop, on the same ctx) stops with it, leaving the pod no backstop either. The drain exists precisely because new requests are still routed to the pod for that window, so for BROKER_DRAIN_SECONDS (5 by default, up to 120) the one pod the load balancer is still choosing serves the old tags, with nothing able to narrow them. Measured on two hand-started binaries: control, neither signalled — retag the store, POST /v1/secrets/AUTO_READ_TOKEN/reread at A, and both pods log the refusal (A +1, B +1). Same fixture with B under SIGTERM and BROKER_DRAIN_SECONDS=30: B answers GET /healthz 503 SHUTTING_DOWN, still answers POST /v1/secrets/AUTO_READ_TOKEN/reread 200 and GET /v1/settings 200, and A's reread gives A +1 and B +0. Red test: packages/envoy/cmd/broker/multiprocess_test.go, TestTwoBrokers/8_ADrainingPodStillTakesAPeersReread, in commit 83e394c11d93. Fails now: `cd packages/envoy && go test -tags multiprocess -count=1 -run 'TestTwoBrokers/8' ./cmd/broker` reports "10s and 10.021s after its SIGTERM, the draining process ... had not reread AUTO_READ_TOKEN, which ... was told to reread and did — while ... still answered GET /v1/settings 200". Verified fixable: running the listener on context.WithCancel(context.WithoutCancel(ctx)) and cancelling it after srv.Shutdown, applied to a scratch copy of main.go, made the row pass in 27 ms, and the file was restored.

proof.criterion: A test in this repository runs two broker processes against one database and covers two concurrent refreshes of one refresh token, two concurrent device-code exchanges, a reread on one process taking effect on the other, and two processes migrating at once.
proof.surface: The repository's own two-process harness against a real Postgres 17.11 server this pod runs (BROKER_TEST_DATABASE_URL), which starts real cmd/broker binaries and drives them over HTTP.

proof.criterion: On SIGTERM the program fails its health check while it keeps serving, long enough for Kubernetes to stop sending it traffic, and only then stops accepting; the shutdown budget is at least the request deadline.
proof.surface: Two cmd/broker binaries built from this workspace and started by hand on one Postgres database of their own, with the production-shaped environment (BROKER_PUBLIC_URL, BROKER_UI_TOKEN, BROKER_SECRETS_PREFIX, BROKER_SECRETS_KMS_KEY_ARN, BROKER_FAKE_SECRETS_FILE), driven with curl and read from their own logs — not through the Go test.
proof.command: go build -o /tmp/hand/broker ./cmd/broker; then BROKER_DRAIN_SECONDS=20 ./broker, kill -TERM <pid>, and curl http://127.0.0.1:13382/healthz, /v1/settings and POST /v1/secrets/AUTO_READ_TOKEN/reread inside the drain
proof.observed: Boot logs `INFO broker stop budget drain=5s shutdown=60s total=65s` as its first line (and `drain=20s shutdown=60s total=80s`, `drain=120s shutdown=60s total=180s`, `drain=0s shutdown=60s total=60s` for those values). After SIGTERM the log reads `INFO broker draining drain=20s`; GET /healthz answers 503 {"code":"SHUTTING_DOWN","error":"the broker is shutting down and is no longer taking new traffic"} while GET /v1/settings answers 200 and POST /v1/secrets/AUTO_READ_TOKEN/reread — a route that takes the policy writer lock and reads the store — answers 200 {"name":"AUTO_READ_TOKEN","served":true} on a connection opened after the signal. With a 30 s drain, a second SIGTERM 0.5 s in logs `INFO broker: a second signal ended the drain early` and the process exits 0.52 s after the first signal. Boundary values are refused by the real binary before it binds: 121, -1, abc and 1.5 each exit on `broker: fatal error="BROKER_DRAIN_SECONDS must be a whole number between 0 and 120, got …"`; 120 and 0 boot.
proof.negativeControl: The same binary with BROKER_DRAIN_SECONDS=0 logs `drain=0s shutdown=60s total=60s` and exits 29 ms after its SIGTERM with no serving window at all, so the window above comes from the flag. A `jj`-restored scratch build is not involved: the two runs differ in that one variable.

proof.criterion: A reread reaches every pod serving the same database (for a pod that is not stopping), and the receiving pod's listener survives losing its Postgres connection.
proof.surface: The same two hand-started cmd/broker binaries on one database, driven with curl, with the fake secret store retagged under them and each pod's own log as the observable (the policy logs `agent secret policy refused` on every store read of a secret whose owner tag is gone).
proof.command: write the store with the owner tag removed; curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:13381/v1/secrets/AUTO_READ_TOKEN/reread (pod A only); then psql -c "select pg_terminate_backend(pid) … where query like 'listen %'" and repeat
proof.observed: A answers 200 {"name":"AUTO_READ_TOKEN","served":false,"reason":"owner-tag-missing"} at 03:14:51.610 and pod B — never called — logs the same refusal by 03:14:51.642, 32 ms later, against a five-minute reload. After both LISTEN backends are terminated from psql, B logs `WARN broker: a Postgres listener has no connection; redialing … attempt=1 wait_ms=1335` and then `INFO broker: listening for the other pods' secret rereads` 1 s later, and the next reread at A again reaches B. A third party writing the channel directly (`notify broker_secret_reread, 'not json at all'` and a sender-only object) is dropped with one WARN each, `payload_bytes` and no payload text, the process stays up, and a well-formed notification sent after them still drives a reread. Two rereads of one name sent to both pods at the same moment both answer 200, with no 5xx and no stall. A pod that is itself draining still SENDS its fan-out: a reread served by a signalled A drove B's reread.
proof.negativeControl: With the store already retagged and no reread call at all, 4 s passed and neither pod logged a refusal (A +0, B +0): the file edit alone changes nothing, so the 32 ms line above is the fan-out and not a reload or a re-read on next use.

notesForTheImplementer: store.Close (internal/broker/store/store.go:163) has no caller in cmd/broker — only storetest and internal/broker/reread's test. The listener pool it closes is therefore never closed in production; the process exits instead, so nothing leaks in a real run, but the simplify-pass justification ("leaked a pgxpool health-check goroutine per store") holds only for tests.

The GCP arithmetic in GCPRereadOverallLimit's comment and in operate.md's "Halved reread limits" paragraph is wrong in the same way as the constant, and both say the fleet's budget is the one-pod budget divided by the replica count. Whatever divisor the fix lands on, those three places (limits.go's two comments, operate.md, and the PR body's Change bullet) have to say the same thing.

A fix for the draining pod also wants the five-minute policy reload to outlive the signal, not only the listener: policy.NewCurrent's loop runs on the same ctx, so a draining pod has neither the fan-out nor its documented backstop. Red test 8 pins only the fan-out.

Red test 7's two budget figures (4 rereads/s default, 1 reread/s GCP) are written in the row rather than read from internal/broker/api on purpose: they are the share of the store's quota this route is allowed, so reading them from the package under test would make the row pass at any sizing.
